newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia drafts budget cuts, tax reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russia drafts budget cuts, tax reforms.

text.p: The Russian government, facing a budget crisis, meets on Friday to consider two crucial plans -- a new draft tax code and huge spending cuts.
The two major measures could pave way to receiving fresh foreign cash and help the new youthful government to proceed with radical market reforms which President Boris Yeltsin has vowed to support.
Low Russian tax revenues are a major obstacle to a resumption of regular payments by the International Monetary Fund of its $10 billion three-year loan.
The IMF has said it will give no more funds until the cabinet agrees the tax code, aimed at making the convoluted tax system simpler and more workable.
Some foreign investors and the IMF say the code is vital to attract foreign investment.

Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin sounded optimistic on Friday, saying the IMF had agreed to back Russia's 1997 programme with credits and that it was likely to pay out hundreds of millions of dollars delayed for the first quarter next month.
Dubinin's deputy, Sergei Aleksashenko, said the IMF was no longer setting macro-economic targets for Russia, such as beating inflation, and was concentrating instead on structural reforms.
"The IMF considers Russia to be more or less stable," he said.
The IMF has also approved of Russia's new-look cabinet, saying it would be a big plus for Russia during the IMF board May vote on resumption of loan payments.

Yeltsin ordered a major reshuffle in the cabinet last month, giving the two key positions of first deputy premier to Anatoly Chubais, 41, and another reformer, Boris Nemtsov, 37, to help to drag the country's moribund economy out of stagnation.

On Thursday Yeltsin said young people would be the best guarantee of future reforms and that they should be promoted to top government jobs. He also appointed Nemtsov the head of fuel and energy minstry, overseeing one of the world's biggest oil and gas sectors.
Another major issue to be considered by the government on Friday is a concrete plan to cut budgetary spending.
Earlier this month Chubais dismissed the 1997 budget as unrealistic and pledged to cut spending across the board.
Revenues in the first quarter were only 60 percent of budgeted levels.
Under the 1997 budget law, if revenues in any quarter are less than 90 percent of planned, the government must present a bill to the State Duma lower house on sequestering, or cutting spending.

Chubais said budget shortfalls this year could be 100 trillion roubles ($17.4 billion), which he called a "monstrous budget crisis." The 1997 budget foresees 434 trillion roubles of revenues and 529.8 trillion roubles expenditures.

The spending cuts have to be approved by Russia's parliament, dominated by communists and conservatives, and many deputies have already said they will not allow the government to reduce support to the ailing budget sphere and cut social payments.

Millions of Russians who have not received their wages and pensions for months joined a wave of protests last month. Further spending cuts in this sphere, proposed by their hate-figure Chubais, can only aggravate the situation, communists say.

Chubais said the cuts meant realism rather than increased hardship for Russians, and that budget recipients will get not less but more in the third and fourth quarters than they got in the first half of the year.

Senior government officials said that while there was hope that the new tax code will be accepted this year, it was unlikely to be passed in time to serve as the basis for the 1998 budget. Meanwhile, critics say the present draft does not radically improve effectiveness.
Either Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin or Chubais will address parliament about the first quarter 1997 budget, including spending cuts, on May 21.
($ = 5738 Russian Roubles)
